text:
Key Takeaways

Farmwave has appointed Michael K. Stern as Advisor and Member of its Board of Directors, bringing in one of the most experienced executives in digital agriculture.

Stern previously served as CEO of The Climate Corporation, Head of Digital Farming at Bayer Crop Science, and held senior leadership roles at Monsanto for 30 years, including Vice President of Row Crops Americas and President of American Seeds.

Farmwave's Precision Harvest System uses cameras mounted on combine harvesters to count kernel loss every 3 to 5 seconds, delivering real-time in-cab data to operators across corn, soybeans, wheat, and cotton.

The system runs on edge computing, allowing it to function in the field without a reliable internet connection — a practical constraint in most commercial farming environments.

Stern also sits on the Board of Directors of Ohalo Genetics and the Board of Trustees of the Missouri Botanical Garden, and holds a Ph.D. in Chemistry from Princeton University along with 24 U.S. patents.

Stern Joins Farmwave Board as Global Scaling Begins

Agricultural AI company Farmwave has named Michael K. Stern as Advisor and Member of its Board of Directors. Stern, who previously served as CEO of The Climate Corporation and Head of Digital Farming at Bayer Crop Science, joins the company as it prepares to expand its Precision Harvest System into new markets.

Stern brings more than 30 years of executive experience in agricultural technology. During his tenure at Monsanto, he held roles including Vice President of Row Crops Americas, President of American Seeds, and Director of Technology for Agriculture Productivity. In those positions, he oversaw the deployment of digital farming tools across millions of acres worldwide. He currently also serves on the Board of Directors of Ohalo Genetics and the Board of Trustees of the Missouri Botanical Garden. He holds a Ph.D. in Chemistry from Princeton University, has authored 25 scientific publications, and holds 24 U.S. patents.

What Farmwave's Precision Harvest System Does

Farmwave is building AI solutions designed to cut crop losses at harvest, one of the more costly inefficiencies in large-scale grain production. Its Precision Harvest System uses cameras placed at key points on a combine harvester, analyzing images every 3 to 5 seconds to count kernel loss as it happens. The data is delivered directly to operators inside the cab, allowing machinery adjustments in real time across corn, soybeans, wheat, and cotton.

The system is built around edge computing, which means it processes data on the device itself rather than relying on a cloud connection. That design choice makes it viable in field conditions where internet connectivity is intermittent or absent — a common reality in production agriculture. For those tracking how AI is being applied to on-farm machinery and yield management, Farmwave's approach represents one of the more operationally focused deployments in the sector.

In Their Own Words

“Our mission has always been to build technology that actually works for the farmer — solving real problems like harvest loss directly at the edge, without requiring a constant internet connection. Mike's unparalleled expertise in commercializing digital agriculture, combined with his deep understanding of agronomy and farm management, will be invaluable as we scale our operations globally and roll out our next-generation Precision Harvest System.” — Craig Ganssle, Founder and CEO, Farmwave

“The next leap in agricultural productivity is not just about gathering data, but providing farmers with actionable, real-time intelligence precisely when they need it most. Farmwave's edge-AI technology directly addresses a critical and costly pain point in the harvest process. I look forward to working with the board and leadership team to accelerate the company's growth and bring this game-changing technology to more farmers around the world.” — Michael K. Stern, incoming Board Member, Farmwave

text:
Key Takeaways

Circularity Fuels has completed the world's first end-to-end conversion of raw agricultural biogas into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), following a six-month pilot at a California dairy farm of more than 5,000 head near Madera.

The fuel meets ASTM D7566 Annex A1 (FT-SPK) specifications and can be blended at up to 50% with conventional Jet-A fuel in commercial aircraft today.

Internal life-cycle analysis puts the fuel's carbon intensity at -350.7 gCO₂e/MJ under California's regulatory framework — net carbon-negative, with each gallon produced equivalent to removing roughly 100 pounds of CO₂e.

The system uses two modular, skid-mounted reactors — the Ouro bi-reforming reactor and the Aion Fischer-Tropsch synthesis reactor — designed to operate at individual farm scale without pipeline access or expensive biogas cleanup infrastructure.

At commercial scale, Circularity Fuels estimates installed capacity at under $100,000 per barrel-per-day — approximately one-fifth the capital cost of SAF plants currently under construction in Europe — with first commercial deployment targeted for 2027.

From Dairy Waste to Jet Fuel: How Circularity Fuels Did It

Circularity Fuels has announced the completion of what it describes as the world's first end-to-end conversion of raw agricultural biogas into sustainable aviation fuel. The six-month pilot drew biogas directly from the manure digester of a California dairy farm, processing it without pre-treatment through an integrated system developed entirely by the company.

The raw biogas — roughly 65% methane and 35% CO₂ — was fed directly into Circularity's on-site system over thousands of operating hours. The resulting fuel meets ASTM D7566 Annex A1 (FT-SPK) specifications, the international standard required for blending with conventional Jet-A in commercial aircraft. It can be blended at up to 50% with Jet-A fuel and used in existing aircraft today with no engine modifications.

Under California's regulatory framework, internal life-cycle modelling puts the fuel's carbon intensity at -350.7 gCO₂e/MJ — firmly net carbon-negative. The negative figure is driven by avoided methane emissions: by consuming gas that would otherwise be vented or flared, each gallon produced is climate-equivalent to removing roughly 100 pounds of CO₂e from the atmosphere.

The Ouro and Aion Reactors

Circularity's system is built around two modular, skid-mounted reactors designed for the small, distributed scales at which agricultural biogas is actually produced.

The Ouro bi-reforming reactor is an electrified unit that achieved more than 98% methane conversion and more than 90% CO₂ conversion in a single step. High CO₂ content has historically been the main barrier to economical biogas processing — the Ouro reactor addresses this directly. The Aion Fischer-Tropsch synthesis reactor then converts the reformed gas into finished jet fuel on-site.

Because both reactors are modular and designed for farm-scale deployment, the system does not require expensive biogas cleanup infrastructure or proximity to a gas pipeline — removing two of the most significant barriers that have prevented dairy operators from monetizing their biogas output.

Capital Costs That Compete with Fossil Jet Fuel

The pilot puts commercial SAF production within reach at under $100,000 per barrel-per-day of installed capacity at commercial scale — approximately one-fifth the capital cost of SAF plants currently under construction in Europe. That cost structure allows Circularity Fuels to sell its jet fuel at fossil parity even from a first-of-a-kind commercial plant.

The fuel qualifies for both federal and state biofuel incentive programmes, including the EPA's Renewable Fuel Standard and California's Low Carbon Fuel Standard (LCFS) — the same policy mechanisms that enabled renewable natural gas, ethanol, and biodiesel to reach commercial scale. For those following how agricultural waste streams are being converted into commercial energy products, this pilot represents one of the more technically complete proofs of concept to date.

“The hard part of this industry was never designing a theoretical plant that could make SAF. It was proving you could do it continuously, from real biogas, at a cost that pencils. We've now done that. The full stack works end-to-end on real feedstock from a real dairy farm, and the economics put commercial SAF from dairy waste within reach of fossil jet fuel.” — Dr. Stephen Beaton, Founder and CEO, Circularity Fuels

Why Agricultural Biogas Is the Right Feedstock

Agricultural biogas is among the lowest-cost feedstocks available for SAF production, largely because most of it currently goes to waste. The global waste biogas resource is theoretically large enough to supply the entire global jet fuel market, yet most dairy and livestock operations today vent or flare their biogas because conventional cleanup and off-take infrastructure is prohibitively expensive.

Current SAF production meets less than 1% of global aviation fuel demand and is dominated by used cooking oil — a feedstock with limited scalability and significant import dependency. Circularity Fuels targets an abundant, domestic, and largely untapped resource instead.

Circularity Fuels Eyes Commercial Deployment from 2027

With its integrated technology stack validated in the field, Circularity Fuels is preparing for its first commercial-scale build. The company expects to break ground on its first commercial site in 2027, targeting agricultural biogas resources across the United States, Latin America, and Europe.

text:
Soybean and palm oil futures fell sharply on Friday after reports emerged of a possible peace deal between the United States and Iran. Markets reacted positively to the prospect of the opening of the Strait of Hormuz and a de-escalation of the conflict, which caused crude oil prices to fall.

Soybean oil futures in Chicago fell 2.6%, reaching their lowest level since April 20. Palm oil on the Kuala Lumpur exchange lost more than 2% of its value and fell to its lowest level since May 26. The rapeseed market also came under pressure: futures in Paris fell 1.7%.

Analysts attribute this dynamics to the close connection between the energy and biofuel sectors. Lower oil prices are making biofuel production less attractive, which in turn is reducing demand for vegetable oils used as feedstock for biodiesel and other renewable fuels.

Adding to the pressure on the rapeseed market is the fact that this crop is an important feedstock for the production of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), biodiesel and renewable diesel. Expectations of a stabilisation in the crude oil market are causing investors to reconsider the demand outlook for these fuels.

title: How BIRAC is shaping India's biotech startup ecosystem - YourStory.com
description:
New Delhi-based Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) is one of the pillars of this industry.
Several successful biotech startups trace their roots to BIRAC.
Bio-NEST are dedicated centres for biotech startups which bring all the elements to create a new company.
At the same time, there is a need to create a channel which will enable Indian biotech startups to explore the global markets.
In addition, also getting into technology partnerships with global biotech research institutions so that efforts are not wasted in building solutions which are already present.
text:
With the noise around information technology, and now artificial intelligence, developments in other fields in recent years have gone relatively unnoticed. One such area is bioeconomy, an ecosystem that uses biological resources to produce industrial goods. The segment is projected to touch $300 billion by 2030 in India.

New Delhi-based Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) is one of the pillars of this industry. A not-for-profit institution under the Department of Science of Technology, BIRAC has undertaken a multi-pronged approach to nurture entrepreneurs in the biotech industry for the past 14 years.

Several successful biotech startups trace their roots to BIRAC. Cleantech company GPS Renewables, for example, received funding under BIRAC’s Biotechnology Ignition Grant. The company, which makes compressed biogas, 2g ethanol, sustainable aviation fuel, recently raised Rs 635 crore.

Another startup is Secunderabad-based Kritsnam Technologies, which makes smart water usage systems that have been implemented across 50,000 hectares of agricultural land.

Haystack Analytics is a Mumbai-based genomics based clinical diagnostics startup whose AI platform enables faster and accurate diagnosis of infectious diseases, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and genetic disorders.

In an interaction with YourStory, former BIRAC Managing Director Jitendra Kumar said, “We dissected the pathway of biotech innovation, analysed it, mapped it and thought wherever there is a gap and requirement, we will provide support.”

(At the time of publishing this article, Jitendra Kumar stepped down from his role as BIRAC MD and is expected to join IIT Hyderabad as R&D advisor)

The institute zeroed on key requirements such as capital, dedicated space, mentors, networks and market access.

Incubation centres

Kumar said their analysis showed that while academic institutions were cradles for deeptech innovation, they didn’t have a dedicated space for scientists and entrepreneurs to build their startups.

This led to BIRAC setting up the Bio-incubation centres called Bio-NEST in the late 2000 at more than 70 locations. Bio-NEST are dedicated centres for biotech startups which bring all the elements to create a new company. They are like plug-and-play facilities offering dedicated space, technical and business mentorship, industry and investor connections, networking platforms etc..

The Bio-NEST network has expanded to 75 bio-incubators, collectively supporting more than 2,500 biotech startups and entrepreneurs working across diverse domains such as healthcare, diagnostics, medical devices, agriculture, industrial biotechnology, bioinformatics, and environmental biotechnology.

Funding channels

As with any business, capital remains a critical challenge for biotech startups. BIRAC has several programmes that support companies at various stages: from incubation all the way to the market launch.

The Biotechnology Ignition Grant (BIG) is the flagship early-stage funding programme. This scheme offers grant-in-aid of up to Rs 50 lakh for a period of 18 months, enabling entrepreneurs to translate their ideas into proof-of-concept. The programme is implemented through a network of 8 mature BioNEST incubators (BIG Partners).

The Sustainable Entrepreneurship and Enterprise Development (SEED), Fund launched in 2016, provides early-stage capital assistance to biotech startups. The fund serves as the first equity-based financial support of up to Rs 30 lakh for startups that have reached the PoC stage. This support enables startups to graduate to a level where they are able to raise investments from other sources like venture capital firms.

The LEAP Fund (Launching Entrepreneurial Driven Affordable Products), launched in 2018, accelerates commercialisation of innovative biotech solutions through targeted equity support. Startups under this programme can access up to Rs 100 lakh for product validation, scale-up, and market deployment.

Biotech Fund of funds – AcE (Accelerating Entrepreneurs) is promoted by DBT under the aegis of Make in India initiative, and implemented by BIRAC. Today, AcE fund supports 16 Alternate Investment Funds (AIF) daughter funds who have invested Venture capital of Rs 1200 crore in 93 Start-ups, SMEs.

The Contract Research Scheme (CRS) was launched by BIRAC in 2012 to bridge the gap between academia and industry. The scheme promotes validation of a product/technology (developed by academia) by an industry partner.

Early Translation Accelerator (ETA) is a strategic initiative aimed at bridging the critical gap between laboratory discoveries and market-ready products by supporting early-stage translational research.

Turning point

During the COVID-19 crisis, BIRAC identified startups, academic institutions and companies that had potential solutions to address the challenges. Out of 1073 proposals, a total of 120 proposals were recommended for funding out of which 46 proposals were recommended to be supported by BIRAC. The Covid-19 mRNA vaccine developed by Gennova Biopharmaceuticals saw BIRAC providing the clinical and phase -1 support.

“Many of these things came from our funded programmes and it has come to public imagination that biotech can do wonders especially after Covid,” remarked Kumar.

Building an ecosystem

BIRAC has been building an ecosystem bringing together every stakeholder onto a single platform. This includes entrepreneurs, venture capitalists, pharmaceutical companies, research bodies and academic institutions.

Today, through the various programmes of BIRAC, around 900 new products across categories have been developed and out in the market. Majority of these products are in the healthcare space, followed by medical devices with sprinkling of biotechnology, agritech, environment etc. Besides, it has led to the filing of more than 1,300 IPs.

However, there is much more to be done if the country needs to fully realise the potential of bio-economy as Kumar says, “I think the next revolution will happen through industrialisation of biology.”

According to Kumar, BIRAC’s incubation centres network which now stands at around 100, needs to be strengthened. Other countries like China, the US or Europe have thousands of such centres.

On the funding ecosystem for these biotech startups, Kumar believes a mechanism has to evolve where there is continuous flow of capital to these entrepreneurs instead of having a project based approach.

Also, the country needs a platform which will attract biotech startups outside India to come and set up their base in the country, especially those with Indian diaspora connection. At the same time, there is a need to create a channel which will enable Indian biotech startups to explore the global markets. In addition, also getting into technology partnerships with global biotech research institutions so that efforts are not wasted in building solutions which are already present.

Kumar believes the pipeline of biotech startups is still not very strong enough for investors to put in their capital and called for creating entrepreneurs in residence-like programmes to encourage the academics to take up the startup route.

Given the importance of bio-economy, the BIRAC MD believes there has to be a mission to reduce the dependence on imported critical raw materials.

Kumar believes given the fast-paced developments in the world of bio-economy there is an urgent need to create a regulatory framework.

“Whatever growth we are envisaging for our country must be a sustainable, circular and net zero economy,” says Kumar.

Throughout 2026, the total volume fuelled should reach 5,000 cubic metres.

According to the gateway, this initiative strengthens its decarbonisation strategy and will help ensure Salvador Bahia maintains its Level 5 status in ACI’s Airport Carbon Accreditation programme.

Alessandra Reis, environmental manager at VINCI Airports in Brazil, said: “The adoption of more sustainable fuels reinforces our commitment to reducing emissions and building an increasingly efficient operation aligned with the transformations of global aviation.

In addition to air operations, the airport has also begun studies to test the use of biodiesel in operational equipment at the terminal. If the results are positive, the expectation is to gradually expand the initiative to the entire operational fleet.

text:
Certas Energy is ramping up its national HVO infrastructure with a £1.5 million (€1.76m) investment to redevelop five HGV refuelling bunkers over the next 12 months — a move that positions the company at the forefront of the UK’s transition to low‑carbon liquid fuels.

The programme has already begun with a £500,000 (€586,000) overhaul of the Alconbury bunker in Cambridgeshire, completed in May. The site is the first to receive a full upgrade of pumps, pipework, security systems and digital card‑reader technology, alongside a major expansion of alternative fuel capability.

Crucially, Alconbury is now Certas Energy’s 17th bunker to offer Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO) — a milestone that underscores the rapid growth in demand for drop‑in renewable diesel across the UK’s haulage and logistics sectors. The company’s 30‑site network is steadily being re‑engineered to support operators seeking immediate, scalable carbon‑reduction options without replacing existing fleets.

Reopened to drivers on 14 May, the upgraded site now features eight high‑speed nozzles capable of dispensing up to 120 litres per minute, cutting dwell times and improving fleet efficiency. Diesel, AdBlue and compatibility with all major digital fuel cards — including Certas Energy’s own FuelTapp — ensure operators retain full flexibility while gaining access to lower‑carbon fuel choices.

The redevelopment also includes an £80,000 (€94,000) investment in a modernised drive‑through truck wash delivered in partnership with UK Truck Clean.

Mike Heaton, head of estate development at Certas Energy, said: “Investment in the existing bunker infrastructure is as important as expanding and building new sites. We want to make sure that every location we operate is equipped for the future, including the ability to offer new fuels, while keeping the refuelling process smooth, efficient and comfortable for HGV drivers on UK roads.”

Heaton added that modernising equipment, strengthening security and maximising uptime are central to preparing the network for the UK’s fuel‑transition period. Further upgrades to Alconbury — including a revamped shop and full Certas Energy rebrand — are scheduled for August 2026.

Alongside the bunker programme, Certas Energy is expanding its truckstop estate, adding two new sites in 2026. Each will replicate the award‑winning facilities and enhanced security standards pioneered at The Stop at The Hollies, with more locations expected to follow as the company builds a nationwide network ready for the shift to alternative fuels.

title: Four Firms Create SAF Venture at the Port of Dunkirk | Procurement Magazine
description:
Technip Energies, Airbus, Safran and Tereos have formed an agreement to establish Rebound, a joint venture focused on sustainable aviation fuel production at the Port of Dunkirk in France.
According to the SAF Coalition, Sustainable Aviation Fuel can reduce lifecycle GHG emissions by 80% to 100% compared to fossil fuels.

EU mandates for aviation According to Airbus, SAF is widely recognised as the primary lever to decarbonise aviation.
By producing advanced ethanol from agricultural and forestry residues, the process creates drop-in aviation fuel.
text:
Technip Energies, Airbus, Safran and Tereos have formed an agreement to establish Rebound, a joint venture focused on sustainable aviation fuel production at the Port of Dunkirk in France. The project aims to develop one of Europe's largest facilities of its type.

According to the SAF Coalition, Sustainable Aviation Fuel can reduce lifecycle GHG emissions by 80% to 100% compared to fossil fuels. The reduction depends on the production process and feedstock used.

Alcohol-to-Jet production pathway

The Rebound project will use the Alcohol-to-Jet technological pathway to produce approximately 145,000 tonnes of SAF each year. This volume could position the facility as a contributor to European energy sovereignty.

The partners have committed to funding the project's development phase. This includes engineering studies and other activities that require consideration before a final investment decision.

"Sustainable Aviation Fuel is one of the most critical levers to decarbonise aviation, and the Alcohol-to-Jet pathway offers a credible, scalable route to get there," says Benjamin Lechuga, Chief Strategy and Sustainability Officer of Technip Energies.

"With Rebound, we are putting into practice our strategy to capture greater value through adjacent business models, originating and developing projects in fast-growing energy transition markets alongside recognised industry leaders such as Airbus, Safran and Tereos.

"We look forward to advancing this project with the engineering rigour and disciplined execution that define Technip Energies."

EU mandates for aviation

According to Airbus, SAF is widely recognised as the primary lever to decarbonise aviation. Under the European Union's ReFuelEU aviation regulation, SAF blending mandates will rise progressively.

The mandates will reach 6% by 2030 and 70% by 2050. This could mean an eightfold increase in demand between 2030 and 2050.

The ReFuel initiative forms part of the EU's Fit for 55 package to meet emissions reduction targets of 55% by 2030. Key goals of the initiative include:

a share of 70% of SAF in all EU airports by 2050

a 1.2% share of synthetic aviation fuels in all EU airports from 2030

by 2050, a 35% share of synthetic aviation fuels in all EU airports.

"The Rebound project is a vote of confidence in SAF and in Europe's ability to be a leader in the journey to decarbonise aviation," says Julie Kitcher, Chief Sustainability Officer and Communications of Airbus.

"With renewable energy facing global headwinds, Airbus will work with our partners to open up an abundant new SAF pathway, Alcohol-to-Jet fuel, in France."

Advanced ethanol conversion

AtJ is an emerging aviation product that converts advanced ethanol into a fuel option. By producing advanced ethanol from agricultural and forestry residues, the process creates drop-in aviation fuel.

This allows for blending with conventional jet fuel and can be used in existing engines and aircraft. Julie adds: "This project aims to increase the availability of lower-carbon fuels, contribute to reducing aviation emissions and strengthen Europe's energy supply security, while creating a new job market.

"I am delighted that Airbus is a partner in the Rebound project, which is a vital step forward for the SAF ecosystem in Europe."

Partner roles and responsibilities

In the project development phase, Technip Energies will act as the lead developer and engineering service provider. This allows for technological scaling expertise to be brought to the project.

Airbus and Safran are joining Rebound as industrial partners, offtake facilitators and potential SAF off-takers. Tereos aims to supply and source the advanced ethanol required for the venture.

"We are delighted to contribute, through Rebound, to the emergence of the Alcohol-to-Jet industry in France, supporting the decarbonization of the aviation sector," says Jérôme Bos, Chief Strategy Officer of Tereos. "This project is fully aligned with Tereos' mission to develop low-carbon industrial value chains by creating value from agricultural production.

"Tereos will bring to the project its expertise and industrial assets dedicated to the production of advanced ethanol. It also provides a strong illustration of the development of a bioeconomy rooted in French and European agricultural production."

Development process and timeline

The joint venture covers the entire value chain from feedstock supply to aviation end use. The partners aim to progress through a disciplined, stage-gated development process.

Steps ahead include selecting the technology licensor and permitting activities. The partners will launch pre-FEED and FEED activities, finalise feedstock supply and SAF offtake agreements, and secure financing for construction of the asset.

"Developing Sustainable Aviation Fuel at scale is essential for decarbonising air transport," says Nathalie Stubler, Chief Sustainability Officer of Safran.

"This ambitious project brings together leading French and European expertise, supporting the emergence of a competitive SAF industry.

"By joining forces with our partners, Safran reaffirms its commitment to innovation and environmental responsibility, fully aligned with our strategy to reduce CO₂ emissions and support the energy transition in aviation. This commitment is reflected in our investments, through Safran Corporate Ventures, in the development of sustainable solutions for the aviation industry of tomorrow."

The finalisation of the joint venture is expected to occur in the second half of 2026. This remains subject to customary closing conditions and approvals.

title: Aviation fuel from CO₂: Finnair supports eSAF pilot
description:
Only after that can the fuel be blended with fossil aviation fuel.
Finnair joined the project primarily to support the development of the technology and its introduction, and to bring the airline's perspective into the development work.
A significant step in the development of eSAF Synthetic aviation fuel, or eSAF, is seen as a promising option for reducing aviation emissions.
In the future, the role of eSAF may grow significant if costs decrease, and the technology develops fast enough.
From 2030 it will also cover synthetic eSAF, and by 2050 sustainable fuels must make up 70% of aviation fuel, half of which must be eSAF.
text:
"We want to show that Finland has the necessary raw materials, biogenic carbon dioxide, hydrogen and energy, as well as the necessary operators to produce synthetic aviation fuel," says Tuomo Karppinen, who works as a project manager at Finnair in the pilot.

Technological readiness plays a crucial role

To date, Liquid Sun has produced a so-called crude SAF intermediate at its pilot plant in Espoo, from which certified eSAF will be refined in the next process phase. Only after that can the fuel be blended with fossil aviation fuel.

Once all the key steps in terms of fuel use have been certified and the fuel has been found to be safe, Finnair's goal is to fly a commercial flight with fuel that contains synthetic eSAF produced in the pilot.

"If the flight will be implemented, it will hopefully serve as a springboard for longer-term development work and provide visibility for eSAF developers, which in turn will help attract funding for projects in the field," Tuomo says.

Finnair joined the project primarily to support the development of the technology and its introduction, and to bring the airline's perspective into the development work. The project also aims to highlight practical challenges.

"We know that the bottleneck in eSAF production at the moment is the demonstration of technical readiness. In addition, we want to transparently highlight the bottlenecks that we still need to solve in building the ecosystem. For example, one of the key questions to consider is where renewable fuel should be blended and how it can be efficiently refueled into aircraft," says Tuomo.

A significant step in the development of eSAF

Synthetic aviation fuel, or eSAF, is seen as a promising option for reducing aviation emissions. Estimates suggest that it could significantly reduce fossil carbon emissions over the full fuel lifecycle, when produced using renewable electricity and captured CO₂.

However, there are challenges along the way. So far, technology is still in its early stages, and production has not been scaled up to an industrial scale. In addition, the production of eSAF requires significant amounts of renewable electricity and raw materials such as hydrogen and carbon dioxide, the capture of which is currently expensive.

What is special about Liquid Sun's project is cost-effectiveness. They have developed a patented solution that can reduce the energy requirement in production.

"Their technology is so-called low-temperature technology, which reduces the need for energy and makes process optimization more flexible, for example, by enabling the use of cheap exchange electricity. In the future, this may enable more cost-efficient production than with current technologies," Tuomo points out.

A key role in Finnair's sustainability work

Sustainable aviation fuels play a key role in achieving Finnair's climate targets, but according to Tuomo, from the point of view of achieving the targets, a lot depends on the price development of the fuel and the maturity and scalability of the technology.

"The single biggest way to reduce emissions is the use of renewable aviation fuels. That is why we want to do everything possible to support eSAF production and technology. We alone burn about a million tonnes of fuel a year, so there certainly is demand. In 2030, the EU will introduce an eSAF blending obligation, which means that eSAF must be available and in use – but at the moment, there is not yet enough production," Tuomo points out.

In the future, the role of eSAF may grow significant if costs decrease, and the technology develops fast enough. The experts involved in the project have a unique opportunity to follow the development of technology closely.

"What inspires me the most is to see the progress of startups and technology development in practice. They have a genuine desire to make things happen – and when they commit to something, solutions are found," Tuomo concludes.

Frequently asked questions about eSAF

What is eSAF? eSAF is synthetic sustainable aviation fuel made from carbon dioxide, water and renewable electricity. It has the same chemical properties as conventional jet fuel, so it works in today's aircraft without modifications. The name stands for electro Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

What is the difference between SAF and eSAF? SAF is the umbrella term for all sustainable aviation fuel. Bio-based SAF is made from feedstocks such as used cooking oil and other waste materials, while eSAF is produced synthetically from captured carbon dioxide and hydrogen made with renewable electricity. eSAF is one type of SAF.

How is eSAF made? Renewable electricity splits hydrogen from water, and that hydrogen is combined with captured carbon dioxide to form synthetic, liquid aviation fuel. In Finland, carbon dioxide can be captured, for example, from emissions from the forest industry and biogas plants, making it bio-based.

How much does eSAF reduce emissions? It has been estimated (ICCT, Project SkyPower) that eSAF could reduce fossil carbon emissions by over 90% across the full fuel lifecycle—from production and distribution to use—when produced using renewable electricity and captured CO₂. The final emissions reduction depends on how the feedstocks and the electricity used in production are sourced.

Why isn't eSAF widely used yet? The technology is still in its early stages and production has not been scaled to an industrial level. Making eSAF requires large amounts of renewable electricity along with hydrogen and carbon dioxide, which are still expensive to capture. For now, only small volumes are available.

What is the EU eSAF blending mandate? The EU blending mandate requires the share of renewable aviation fuels to rise gradually. From 2030 it will also cover synthetic eSAF, and by 2050 sustainable fuels must make up 70% of aviation fuel, half of which must be eSAF.

What is Finnair doing to advance eSAF? Finnair advances eSAF by taking an active part in developing it and building the ecosystem around it. We are involved in the Finnish company Liquid Sun's eSAF pilot together with ABB, Fortum and Finavia, with the goal of showing that synthetic aviation fuel can be produced in Finland. We also help the wider market take shape through the SAF work of the Finnish Hydrogen Cluster.

text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Korea Environment Corporation (K-eco), in collaboration with the Embassy of the Republic of Korea in Malaysia, successfully organized the Biogas Towards Carbon Neutrality Workshop today at Pullman Kuala Lumpur City Centre Hotel, bringing together government officials, industry leaders, researchers, and environmental experts from both countries to strengthen cooperation in biogas development, greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction, and carbon neutrality, according to a press release.

The workshop served as a platform for policy dialogue, knowledge exchange, and partnership building between Malaysia and the Republic of Korea in support of global climate action and sustainable development goals. Approximately 90 participants attended the event, representing government agencies, international organizations, research institutions, and private sector companies from both countries.

The event was officiated by YB Datuk Chang Lih Kang, Minister of Science, Technology and Innovation (MOSTI), and attended by H.E. Yeo Seung-bae, Ambassador of the Republic of Korea to Malaysia, Mr. Seo Seung-Myeong, Director General of Korea Environment Corporation (K-eco), and Mr. Mohd Khairul Fidzal Abdul Razak, Chief Executive Officer of Malaysian Bioeconomy Development Corporation (Bioeconomy Corporation).

A major highlight of the event was the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between Korea Environment Corporation and Bioeconomy Corporation. The MOU establishes a framework for cooperation in the biogas sector, including knowledge sharing, technical collaboration, policy exchange, capacity building, project development, research and innovation, and the promotion of sustainable bioenergy solutions.

H.E. Yeo Seung-bae, Ambassador of the Republic of Korea to Malaysia, highlighted the longstanding partnership between the two countries and the importance of collaborative climate action and low-carbon development.

“Climate change is a global challenge that requires international cooperation and collective action. The Republic of Korea highly values its partnership with Malaysia in promoting sustainable development and carbon neutrality. I am pleased to see government agencies, industry leaders, and experts from both countries come together to discuss practical solutions in the biogas sector and explore further cooperation under shared climate goals.”

The Republic of Korea has accumulated extensive experience in transforming food waste, livestock manure, and sewage sludge into renewable energy resources, while Malaysia possesses significant biomass and biogas potential through its agricultural and palm oil sectors, including POME-based biogas. The workshop highlighted opportunities to combine these complementary strengths through future technical cooperation, investment, and commercialization initiatives.

Mr. Mohd Khairul Fidzal Abdul Razak, Chief Executive Officer of Bioeconomy Corporation, noted that the collaboration comes at a time of growing global interest in sustainable bioenergy and circular economy solutions.

“Globally, billions of tonnes of organic waste are generated each year, yet less than five per cent of sustainable feedstock potential is currently utilised for biogas and biomethane production. This presents a significant opportunity for countries like Malaysia and the Republic of Korea to work together in transforming waste into value through innovation, knowledge exchange, and expertise sharing, while unlocking new economic and environmental pathways for both countries.”

In his opening remarks, Mr. Seo Seung-Myeong, Director General of K-eco, emphasized the growing importance of biogas as a practical solution for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and supporting the transition towards a circular and low-carbon economy. He highlighted K-eco’s extensive experience in implementing Korea’s environmental policies, including greenhouse gas reduction programs, support for the Korea Emissions Trading Scheme (K-ETS), international cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, and the promotion of biogas production by converting organic waste into renewable energy resources.

“Korea and Malaysia share a common commitment to building a sustainable future. Through today’s MOU and workshop, we hope to expand practical cooperation in biogas development, greenhouse gas reduction, and the low-carbon transition, while contributing to carbon neutrality and long-term environmental sustainability in both countries,” said Mr. Seo.

Mr. Seo also reaffirmed K-eco’s commitment to supporting environmental cooperation across Southeast Asia and promoting partnerships among governments, local authorities, research institutions, and industry stakeholders. The successful organization of the Biogas Towards Carbon Neutrality Workshop and the signing of the MOU reflect the shared commitment of Malaysia and the Republic of Korea to advance bilateral cooperation and accelerate the transition towards a more sustainable, resilient, and low-carbon future.

text:
Exolum has commenced operations at the aviation fuel storage and distribution facilities and the hydrant network at Cristiano Ronaldo International Airport in Madeira, Portugal, managed by ANA (VINCI Group).

text:
בפינה מרוחקת של משחטת עוף הנגב, בסמוך לעיר אופקים, עומדת מכולה שדפנותיה הוסרו. בקצה האחד שלה מותקן משפך מתכת ענק, ובקצה השני — צינור שממנו אמור לזרום תחליף לנפט. בתוך מסגרת המכולה מותקנת שורה של מכלים וצינורות. זהו המתקן המסחרי הראשון מסוגו שהקימה חברת נקי (NAKI), לאחר עשרות הרצות מוצלחות במעבדה.

ביקרתי במקום במהלך סיור של קהילת החדשנות באנרגיה Ignite The Spark, שעסק בתעשיית האנרגיה בנגב המערבי. עוד לפני שעלינו לאוטובוס במתקן של חברת תש"א (תשתיות אנרגיה) הלאומית, הכין אותנו המייסד והמנכ"ל, ברק מנבר, לריח העז שאנחנו צפויים לו. ואכן, כמה מהמשתתפים שירדו מהאוטובוס מיהרו לחזור אליו כעבור דקות ספורות, עוד לפני שהחל ההסבר.

"התחליף שאנחנו מייצרים פה יכול להחליף את הנפט הגולמי בבתי הזיקוק מבלי שהם יידרשו לבצע התאמה כלשהי במתקנים שלהם", מסביר מנבר, שייסד את החברה יחד עם מיכאל קופליק, המכהן כ–CTO. בנקי פיתחו טכנולוגיה שמאפשרת להפיק מפסולת אורגנית שמן המשמש תחליף לנפט, שאותו הם מכנים Mida Oil. במקום שהפסולת מהמשחטה תופנה להטמנה, היא נהפכת למשאב בעל ערך כלכלי. תחליף הנפט הזה מיועד להגיע לבתי הזיקוק, שם הוא ישמש בעיקר לייצור דלק מטוסים בר־קיימא (Sustainable Aviation Fuel, או SAF).

נקי מבקשת לתת מענה לרגולציה העולמית שמחמירה והולכת, ובראשה זו של האיחוד האירופי. החל מ–2030, כל מטוס שינחת בנמל התעופה של האיחוד יחויב להשתמש בתמהיל דלק המכיל SAF — תחילה אחוזים בודדים ממנו (2%), אך השיעור יעלה בהדרגה. חברות תעופה שלא יעמדו בתקנה יידרשו לשלם מסים גבוהים יותר.

"חברות תעופה נדרשות כיום למצוא פתרונות לדלק נקי, ולרגולציה הזאת יש השפעה רוחבית על העולם כולו", מסביר מנבר. "השאיפה היא להביא את עולם התעופה לאפס פליטות עד 2050. לפי ההערכות, המשמעות היא שהעולם יידרש לכ–450 מיליון טונה של דלק מטוסים בר קיימא בשנה", הוסיף.

לא תלויים בשרשרת האספקה הבינלאומית

לפי דו"ח סוכנות האנרגיה הבינלאומית (IEA), פליטות גזי החממה ממגזר התעופה הן כ–2.5% מסך הפליטות הגלובליות — נתח שיהיה קשה לצמצם. בעוד בענפי תחבורה אחרים המבוססים על דלקים — כמו רכבים פרטיים — יש פתרונות חשמליים זמינים, למטוסים מסחריים גדולים אין כרגע חלופה חשמלית ריאלית. לכן, המענה המרכזי הוא החלפת הדלק הסילוני המזוקק מנפט בדלק בר קיימא ממקורות חלופיים.

אחד האתגרים המרכזיים בייצור SAF הוא מציאת חומרי גלם זמינים בכמויות מספקות, שאינם מתחרים בגידולי חקלאות למזון או דורשים שימושי קרקע נרחבים (כמו גידול סויה לדלק). כאן נכנסות שאריות העוף של משחטת עוף הנגב.

המתקן נמצא בימים אלה לקראת תחילתו של פיילוט, שבמסגרתו הוא אמור לטפל בכ–700 טונה של פסולת (בוצה) בחודש. לפני שהשאריות מגיעות למתקן של נקי, מפעל עוף הנגב מפריד מהן את הפסולת המימית; המים מופנים למתקן טיהור השפכים הצמוד למשחטה, ושאר הבוצה המרוכזת מועברת אל מכולת הטיפול.

"אנחנו יושבים בין שתי תעשיות שכל אחת מהן מזהמת בדרכה, ומצליחים להפוך את שתיהן לקצת יותר ירוקות", אומר מנבר. "בסופו של דבר העולם עדיין תלוי בנפט, והשאלה היא אם נוכל לעזור לו להיות מעט יותר נקי. המוצר שלנו הוא נפט שלא מביא איתו את התלות בשרשרת אספקה בינלאומית מורכבת — הוא מיוצר מקומית, באתר עצמו. וזה לא משנה אם מפיקים אותו במשחטה, במפעל גלידה או במפעל שמייצר אוכל מוכן".

להרוויח משני הקצוות

כיום, מפעלים משלמים 150–400 שקל עבור פינוי והטמנה של כל טונת פסולת (בהתאם לסוג הפסולת ולמרחק הפינוי). נקי לוקחת את הפסולת הזאת ומציעה להם פתרון קצה מקומי ומשתלם יותר בתוך המפעל.

"אנחנו מבצעים פירוק של חלבונים ושומנים באמצעות חומרים כימיים שפועלים במערכת סגורה", מפרט מנבר. "החלבונים, שהם כ–80% מהבוצה, מופנים למתקני ביו־גז לייצור חשמל. השומנים, שהם ה–20% הנותרים, מיועדים לבתי הזיקוק".

במסגרת הפיילוט, כ–100 טונה של שומן בחודש אמורות להפוך לשמן המתאים לזיקוק לדלק סילוני — כמות שוות ערך לכ–730 חביות נפט. לשם ההשוואה, ובאופן תיאורטי, כמות השמן שייצר המתקן במשך שנה שלמה תוכל לספק את תפוקת הזיקוק של בית הזיקוק בחיפה (בז"ן) למשך שעה בודדת. ברור שאלה אינן כמויות שישנו לבדן את מפת האנרגיה, אך המטרה אינה להחליף את כל הנפט הגולמי, אלא לספק בשלב הראשון את אותם 2% של רכיב ירוק הדרושים כדי לעמוד ברגולציה האירופית.

"בדקנו את השוק המקומי", מסביר מנבר. "כדי למהול את כל הדלק הסילוני בישראל לרמה של 2% SAF, נדרשות 60–70 טונה של חומר גלם ביום. לשם כך אנחנו צריכים להציב כ–40 מתקנים כאלה במפעלים שונים ברחבי ישראל".

המודל העסקי של נקי בנוי על הכנסה כפולה: החברה גם מציבה את המתקן במפעל ומקבלת תשלום על עצם פינוי והפחתת הפסולת, וגם מוכרת את תחליף הנפט האיכותי לבתי הזיקוק.

להערכת החברה, עלות הייצור של חבית שמן כזאת תהיה כ–35 דולר בלבד, וכל מתקן שיוקם צפוי להחזיר את ההשקעה בו בתוך כשנתיים וחצי. חלק מהיכולת להפחית בצורה דרמטית את עלויות הייצור נובע מהסימביוזה התעשייתית: נקי מנצלת את עודפי החום והקור של מפעל המזון כדי לחסוך באנרגיה הדרושה לתהליך הייצור.

"החזון שלנו הוא לשנות מן היסוד את הדרך שבה התעשייה העולמית מתייחסת לפסולת שלה", מסכם מנבר. "במקום לקבור אותה באדמה ולשלם על כך, אפשר להפוך אותה לדלק ירוק בייצור מקומי, ולקחת חלק במעבר הגלובלי לאנרגיה נקייה יותר".

title: Worley Completes FEED for Alfanar Lighthouse Green Fuels SAF Project in Teesside
description:
Worley has completed Front-End Engineering and Design for Alfanar‘s Lighthouse Green Fuels sustainable aviation fuel project in Teesside, UK.
Lighthouse Green Fuels – Project Background Lighthouse Green Fuels is planned as a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable naphtha refinery at Teesside.
CCS-Enabled Design and Teesside Infrastructure Interfaces The Lighthouse Green Fuels project is designed to be carbon capture and storage (CCS) enabled.
Global Low-Carbon Fuels Market Outlook – CF Intel Analysis Lighthouse Green Fuels sits within a low-carbon fuels market where front-end engineering is doing the hard work of separating investable projects from policy ambition.
Source: Worley Supporting Sources: Alfanar, Lighthouse Green Fuels
text:
Worley has completed Front-End Engineering and Design for Alfanar‘s Lighthouse Green Fuels sustainable aviation fuel project in Teesside, UK.

The completed FEED package moves the project into a more technically defined development phase ahead of a targeted Final Investment Decision by the end of 2027. Once operational, the facility is expected to produce around 180 million litres of sustainable aviation fuel and 30 million litres of renewable naphtha annually, with commercial operations expected in 2032.

Lighthouse Green Fuels – Project Background

Lighthouse Green Fuels is planned as a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable naphtha refinery at Teesside. Alfanar’s project materials describe the development as a brownfield refinery project that will convert sustainably sourced biomass, including forestry, sawmill and agricultural residues, into drop-in aviation fuel.

The project is being developed against the UK SAF mandate, which came into effect in January 2025 and targets SAF reaching 10% of UK jet fuel demand by 2030. Alfanar says this is equivalent to around 1.2 million tonnes of SAF per year, making domestic SAF production capacity a material industrial and fuels infrastructure issue for the UK market.

The planned facility is expected to process more than 1.5 million tonnes per year of sustainably sourced biomass feedstock. The process gasifies feedstock into synthesis gas, cleans the gas stream and uses Fischer-Tropsch synthesis to produce hydrocarbon waxes that are then upgraded into SAF and renewable naphtha.

FEED Scope and Project Definition

Worley’s FEED scope covered feedstock handling, gasification, Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, utilities, storage infrastructure and potential integration with Teesside’s emerging carbon capture and storage network. The engineering work was carried out by Worley’s UK team with support from its Global Integrated Delivery experts in India.

For project delivery teams, the significance of FEED completion is that it converts a process concept into a more defined technical and commercial basis. At this stage, scope, cost, schedule, execution strategy and interface risks become clearer before the project moves toward project financing, procurement and construction commitment.

Worley says the FEED phase is expected to reduce project risk and improve cost, schedule and execution certainty ahead of FID. In practical terms, the next major steps are the investment decision, contracting strategy, major equipment procurement, site execution planning and later notice to proceed milestones.

CCS-Enabled Design and Teesside Infrastructure Interfaces

The Lighthouse Green Fuels project is designed to be carbon capture and storage (CCS) enabled. Alfanar’s project page states that the core plant design removes carbon dioxide from the syngas stream so the Fischer-Tropsch reaction can operate efficiently, creating a high-purity carbon dioxide stream that is suitable for sequestration.

Alfanar also intends to capture carbon dioxide emissions from the on-site integrated power plant and send them to permanent storage. The interface with Teesside’s emerging CCS network is therefore more than an environmental feature; it is part of the industrial integration required for the plant’s low-carbon fuel pathway.

Worley’s scope did not stop at the process units. Feedstock handling, utilities and storage infrastructure are material delivery interfaces for a project of this type, particularly where biomass logistics, gasification, fuel upgrading, tankage, quay access and carbon capture systems need to work as one facility.

Global Low-Carbon Fuels Market Outlook – CF Intel Analysis

Lighthouse Green Fuels sits within a low-carbon fuels market where front-end engineering is doing the hard work of separating investable projects from policy ambition. Similar activity has been noted across early-stage fuels and hydrogen projects, including Technip’s FEED role on Jet Zero’s alcohol-to-jet SAF project in Australia, thyssenkrupp Uhde’s pre-FEED contracts for Fuella’s green ammonia projects in Brazil and Utility Global and SAMJIN E&I advancing the Daejeon H2Gen hydrogen project in South Korea.

The market signal is that alternative fuels projects are moving through increasingly detailed front-end gates before sponsors commit capital. For contractors and suppliers, the opportunity is not only in the future EPC contract packages; it is also in early engineering, process integration, feedstock logistics, storage systems, CCS interfaces and execution planning.

What to Watch

FID pathway: Alfanar is targeting FID by the end of 2027. The key test is whether the completed FEED package supports a financeable execution plan for a large, integrated biomass-to-liquids project.

CCS interface: Potential integration with Teesside’s carbon capture and storage network will be important for the project’s carbon intensity and industrial delivery model.

Supply chain readiness: Biomass feedstock logistics, gasification systems, Fischer-Tropsch units, utilities, storage and construction sequencing will all need to be aligned before major execution can proceed.

Source: Worley

Supporting Sources: Alfanar, Lighthouse Green Fuels

title: Why the Future of Sustainable Aviation Fuel Depends on Digital Feedstock Discovery
description:
For the better part of two decades, the biofuels industry has focused almost exclusively on one side of the equation.
Every refinery announcement, every Sustainable Aviation Fuel mandate, every airline commitment and every net-zero roadmap ultimately depends on one thing.
Every day, families cook meals, fry food and generate waste oil that is often discarded.
However, through the integration of digital collection infrastructure, they can also serve as community recycling centres.
By integrating collection infrastructure directly into operational workflows, these risks can be reduced substantially while simultaneously improving efficiency and traceability.
text:
For the better part of two decades, the biofuels industry has focused almost exclusively on one side of the equation.

We have debated technologies. We have debated refining pathways. We have debated regulations, mandates, carbon accounting methodologies, financing structures, certification systems and supply chains. Billions of dollars have been invested into developing technologies capable of converting waste and residue-based feedstocks into low-carbon fuels. Entire industries have emerged around refining, trading, certification and compliance.

Yet despite all this progress, one fundamental problem remains largely unsolved.

Where will the feedstock come from?

Every refinery announcement, every Sustainable Aviation Fuel mandate, every airline commitment and every net-zero roadmap ultimately depends on one thing. Feedstock.

Without feedstock, there is no renewable diesel.

Without feedstock, there is no Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

Without feedstock, there is no energy transition.

The reality is that the greatest challenge facing our industry today is not refining technology. The technology exists. The capital exists. The demand certainly exists. What does not yet exist at the scale required is a system capable of discovering, aggregating and mobilising enough sustainable feedstock to meet future demand.

For years, feedstock aggregation has been approached largely as a logistics exercise. Companies buy trucks, rent warehouses, hire drivers and attempt to build collection networks. While this approach may have worked when the industry was smaller, it is increasingly proving insufficient for the scale of the challenge that lies ahead.

The future of biofuels will not be won by those with the largest trucks. It will be won by those with the best data. The future belongs to those capable of discovering feedstock that nobody else can see. That is the lesson we have learned at FatHopes Energy over the last fifteen years.

When we first started collecting Used Cooking Oil, our world was relatively straightforward. The majority of available volumes were concentrated within the food and beverage sector. Restaurants, hotels, food courts, industrial kitchens and fast-food chains generated substantial quantities of waste cooking oil and represented the most logical starting point for any collection programme.

Like many others in the industry, we built our business around these commercial generators. We established collection routes, developed relationships with restaurant operators and invested heavily in logistics infrastructure. For many years, this model served us well.

However, as the biofuels industry matured, something began to change. Demand accelerated. What was once a niche industry became a strategic industry. What was once considered alternative became mainstream.

Governments introduced mandates. Airlines committed to decarbonisation targets. Investors began allocating capital. Refineries started appearing across multiple continents. Every new refinery required feedstock. Every new SAF producer required feedstock. Every new renewable diesel facility required feedstock.

Suddenly the same waste streams that had once been overlooked became highly sought after commodities. The challenge was no longer collecting feedstock. The challenge became finding more of it.

As we looked deeper into the problem, we realised something important. The future growth opportunity for our industry was not hidden within large industrial generators. It was hidden within millions of households.

Every day, households across Malaysia produce used cooking oil. Every day, families cook meals, fry food and generate waste oil that is often discarded. Historically, this oil has been poured down drains, thrown into rubbish bins or disposed of without a second thought.

Yet collectively, these small volumes represent one of the largest untapped feedstock resources available anywhere in the world. The problem is not that the resource does not exist. The problem is that it is fragmented.

Recovering twenty tonnes of used cooking oil from a fast-food chain is relatively simple. Recovering twenty tonnes from thousands of households is an entirely different challenge.

Traditional collection systems were never designed for this. The economics do not work. The logistics become overwhelming. The administrative burden becomes immense. The traceability requirements become almost impossible to manage. It was at this point that we realised something that would fundamentally change the direction of our company.

The future of feedstock aggregation would not be built on trucks. It would be built on technology. More specifically, it would be built on digital infrastructure.

For many years, digitalisation has transformed industries such as transportation, banking, retail and hospitality. Consumers now expect real-time visibility, instant transactions and seamless digital experiences in almost every aspect of their lives. Yet within the biofuels industry, many collection systems remained remarkably analogue.

Collection requests were managed through phone calls. Scheduling was coordinated through text messages. Collection records were maintained manually. Traceability often relied on paperwork. Performance data was fragmented across multiple systems. For an industry tasked with delivering one of the most important environmental solutions of our generation, the underlying infrastructure remained surprisingly outdated.

We believed there was a better way.

Almost ten years ago, we began building what has since evolved into a comprehensive digital ecosystem designed specifically for feedstock aggregation. Rather than developing a single application, we created a connected technology stack where every participant within the supply chain could interact through a common digital platform.

The objective was simple. Make feedstock discovery easier. Make feedstock collection more efficient. Make feedstock traceability absolute. Make participation accessible to everyone.

Today, that ecosystem consists of multiple applications serving different stakeholders throughout the value chain.

The Vendor App was developed for commercial generators such as restaurants, hotels, food courts and fast-food operators. Historically, these businesses relied heavily on manual communication whenever collections were required. Managers would call collectors, send messages or wait for routine collection schedules. There was limited visibility, limited accountability and little control over the process.

The Vendor App changed that entirely.

Collection requests can now be initiated instantly. Collection schedules can be managed digitally. Historical collection data is accessible at any time. Environmental impact metrics can be monitored continuously. Most importantly, collection vehicles can be tracked in real time, giving businesses visibility that previously did not exist.

The impact extends beyond convenience. By digitising interactions between generators and collectors, we have created a level of transparency that benefits every participant within the ecosystem.

Supporting this system is our Driver App, which acts as the operational backbone of our collection network. Every day, hundreds of collection vehicles navigate complex routes involving thousands of collection points across multiple regions. Historically, route planning depended heavily on human judgement and experience. While effective to a degree, this approach inevitably resulted in inefficiencies.

The Driver App allows routes to be optimised dynamically. Drivers receive collection assignments digitally. Volumes can be forecast. Vehicle utilisation can be monitored. Navigation support is integrated directly into operational workflows.

The result is lower operating costs, reduced emissions, improved service quality and higher recovery rates. Every unnecessary kilometre avoided improves both economics and sustainability. Every additional litre recovered strengthens the circular economy.

As important as commercial collections remain, the most exciting development within our ecosystem has undoubtedly been the emergence of household participation.

For decades, waste management has been viewed primarily as a disposal exercise. Society generated waste and then attempted to remove it as efficiently as possible. Very little attention was given to the latent value contained within these waste streams.

That mindset is now changing.

Through our Consumer App, households are able to participate directly in the circular economy. Individuals can locate collection points, schedule contributions, track their recycling activities and receive rewards for their participation. More importantly, they gain visibility into the environmental impact of their actions.

What was once considered waste now has value. What was once discarded now generates income. What was once an environmental liability has become a renewable resource. Perhaps the most profound outcome has been behavioural change.

We are witnessing an entire generation beginning to understand that sustainability and economic value are not mutually exclusive. Households are increasingly recognising that responsible environmental behaviour can also create tangible financial benefits.

This shift in mindset may ultimately prove more valuable than the feedstock itself. After all, sustainable industries are not built solely on infrastructure. They are built on participation. They are built on engagement. They are built on trust.

To further expand collection reach, we developed the Ranger App, enabling micro-aggregation at the community level. Rather than relying exclusively on centralised collection infrastructure, communities themselves become active participants in feedstock recovery. Local collection champions can aggregate material, coordinate participation and facilitate collection activities within their neighbourhoods.

This creates a distributed collection network capable of reaching feedstock sources that would otherwise remain inaccessible. In effect, every neighbourhood becomes a potential feedstock hub.

Every household becomes a potential contributor. Every citizen becomes a stakeholder within the energy transition. The implications of this model extend far beyond biofuels. They represent a blueprint for how circular economies can function at scale.

One particularly interesting outcome emerged through our collaboration with petrol station operators. Traditionally, petrol stations exist to distribute fuel. However, through the integration of digital collection infrastructure, they can also serve as community recycling centres.

When households deposit used cooking oil at participating locations, transactions are recorded digitally, rewards are distributed automatically and traceability is maintained throughout the process. What surprised us was the commercial impact.

Locations participating in these programmes experienced significant increases in customer engagement and footfall. Many contributors subsequently spent their rewards within the station’s convenience store, creating additional commercial value for retailers.

For perhaps the first time, sustainability, customer acquisition and commercial performance were aligned within a single ecosystem.

The same principle applies within the fast-food industry, where our collection technologies have significantly reduced the need for manual oil handling. Historically, transferring used cooking oil exposed staff to potential burn risks and operational hazards. By integrating collection infrastructure directly into operational workflows, these risks can be reduced substantially while simultaneously improving efficiency and traceability.

This is often overlooked when discussing innovation. Technology should not only improve margins. Technology should improve lives.

Perhaps the greatest benefit delivered by digital infrastructure is traceability. In an era where sustainability claims are increasingly scrutinised, the ability to verify feedstock origins has become essential. Every litre entering the biofuels supply chain must be accounted for. Every transaction must be transparent. Every participant must be accountable.

Our digital ecosystem enables precisely that. We know who contributed the material. We know where it originated. We know when it was collected. We know where it travelled. We know where it was delivered. This level of visibility creates trust across the entire value chain and strengthens the credibility of sustainable fuels as a whole. It also enables something equally important: accurate emissions measurement.

Because we understand the precise movement of material throughout the supply chain, emissions calculations can move beyond assumptions and approximations. Distances travelled, collection patterns and transportation activities can all be measured with significantly greater precision.

As regulators, investors and airlines demand increasingly sophisticated sustainability reporting, this capability will become indispensable.

Looking ahead, it is becoming increasingly clear that the future leaders of the biofuels industry will not necessarily be those with the largest refineries. They will be those with the strongest feedstock ecosystems. They will be those capable of discovering feedstock others cannot find, recovering feedstock others cannot access and tracing feedstock others cannot verify.

Feedstock discovery is rapidly becoming the most important competitive advantage within the industry. Technology is what makes that possible.

As Malaysia continues to position itself as a leader in sustainable aviation fuel and advanced biofuels, we have a unique opportunity before us. We can build not merely a refining industry, but an entire digital ecosystem capable of becoming the global benchmark for feedstock aggregation.

Imagine a future where every household participates. Every restaurant is digitally connected. Every collection is traceable. Every contributor is rewarded. Every litre recovered contributes towards decarbonising aviation.

That future is no longer theoretical. The foundations are already being built. The question is not whether digitalisation will transform feedstock aggregation. The question is who will lead that transformation.

At FatHopes Energy, we believe the answer begins with connecting every participant within the ecosystem and ensuring that nobody is too small to contribute. Because the future of Sustainable Aviation Fuel does not begin at the refinery.

It begins in the kitchen. It begins in the community. It begins with discovering value where others see waste. And if we get this right, Malaysia and Selangor will not simply participate in the global energy transition. They will become the benchmark by which the rest of the world measures itself.

text:
Savannah-based business jet manufacturer Gulfstream has inaugurated its first dedicated customer support center at Seletar Airport in Singapore, in collaboration with Jet Aviation. This strategic move highlights Gulfstream’s confidence in the Asia-Pacific region, with Singapore positioned as a pivotal hub for the company’s expansion in business aviation.

Strategic Expansion in Asia-Pacific

Lor Izzard, Gulfstream’s Senior Vice President of Support, emphasized Singapore’s significance as a “natural choice given its role as a leading aerospace hub.” The newly established facility, situated within Jet Aviation’s Singapore premises, is staffed by a team of eight Gulfstream professionals, including customer technical managers, materials and quality specialists, a field service representative, and a regional sales manager. Izzard noted that having a dedicated on-site team enables Gulfstream to provide a more seamless and convenient service experience for customers throughout the region.

This support center complements Gulfstream’s existing 5,000-square-foot distribution facility in Singapore, which fulfills over 70% of regional parts orders and maintains an inventory exceeding $70 million in spare parts. This infrastructure not only supports repair operations but also advances Gulfstream’s long-term strategy to expand in-house component support capabilities.

Competitive Landscape and Market Dynamics

Gulfstream’s expansion occurs amid intensifying competition within the Asia-Pacific business aviation maintenance sector. Established competitors such as Bombardier are also enhancing their regional presence; notably, Bombardier recently announced a $100 million, 250,000-square-foot facility at Seletar Aerospace Park. Additionally, private aviation services provider WingsOverAsia has commenced construction on a maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) and innovation facility at Seletar, expected to be operational by 2027. This new facility will enable WingsOverAsia to service larger aircraft, including the Gulfstream G700 as well as Boeing and Airbus corporate jets.

Industry observers are closely monitoring how Gulfstream will leverage its Singapore facility to enhance service offerings and sustain its competitive advantage. The company faces the challenge of differentiating itself in a market where rivals are also investing heavily in customer support and infrastructure. Analysts anticipate that competitors may respond with increased marketing efforts and service improvements to safeguard their market share.

Recent Aircraft Debuts and Regional Commitment

The opening of the Singapore support center follows Gulfstream’s European debut of its next-generation G300 and G400 aircraft at Farnborough Airport, London’s business aviation hub, on June 9. Mark Burns, Gulfstream’s president, highlighted the jets’ “unmatched performance, efficiency and cabin innovation—capabilities that are ideally suited to operators in the region.”

Unveiled in September 2025, the super-midsize G300 features the longest cabin in its class, accommodating up to 10 passengers and offering a range of 3,600 nautical miles at Mach 0.80. The G400 set a city-pair speed record en route to Farnborough, flying 3,250 nautical miles from Washington, D.C., in just over six hours at an average speed of Mach 0.87, utilizing sustainable aviation fuel.

Through the establishment of its Singapore support center and the introduction of new aircraft models, Gulfstream is reaffirming its commitment to growth in the Asia-Pacific region, even as it navigates a dynamic and increasingly competitive market environment.

“Our goal is to strengthen India’s bio-energy ecosystem and align industry priorities with our national climate commitments, including the pledge to achieve net-zero emissions.
“Bio-energy is not merely an alternative fuel source; it is a strategic pillar of India’s green growth story, poised to become a cornerstone of our energy transition.

text:
Bio-energy is emerging as a key pillar of India’s green growth strategy and is set to play a crucial role in the country’s energy transition, Trade Promotion Council of India (TPCI) said on Sunday.

The council, on June 12, gathered policymakers, diplomats, industry leaders, energy experts, innovators, and stakeholders from across the bio-energy ecosystem to deliberate on strategies for accelerating India’s transition towards sustainable and energy-secure growth.

It said that the council has constituted a Bio-Energy Committee to bring together stakeholders across the sector, facilitate dialogue on policy and regulatory reforms, and recommend frameworks to accelerate adoption and unlock investment potential.

“Our goal is to strengthen India’s bio-energy ecosystem and align industry priorities with our national climate commitments, including the pledge to achieve net-zero emissions. Now is the time. Collaboration will be the key. Government, industry, and academia must work together to ensure innovation, affordability, and scalability,” TPCI Chairman Mohit Singla said.

He said that huge opportunities are there in the bio-energy sector, and it will help reduce dependence on fossil fuels while addressing waste management challenges.

From bio-CNG and ethanol blending to biomass power generation, this sector can significantly strengthen India’s clean energy mix, create rural employment and empower farmers, Singla said.

“Bio-energy is not merely an alternative fuel source; it is a strategic pillar of India’s green growth story, poised to become a cornerstone of our energy transition. Energy security, sustainability, climate resilience, and economic growth are no longer separate conversations. They are deeply interconnected,” he added.

Bio-energy is renewable energy derived from biological sources such as agricultural residues, crop waste, animal manure, forestry by-products, municipal organic waste and dedicated energy crops.

It can be converted into various forms of energy, including biofuels like ethanol and compressed biogas (CBG), electricity, heat and sustainable aviation fuel.

title: Thailand Sustainable Aviation Fuel Market Analysis
description:
Thailand’s sustainable aviation fuel industry is shifting from early projects to a rule-based market.
The Department of Energy Business is preparing to introduce new SAF standards and to make blending mandatory in jet fuel from 2026.
Under the framework, Jet A-1 fuel specifications and quality requirements at both production and sale stages will be split into three categories: conventional Jet A-1 fuel, fuel produced through co-hydroprocessing, and conventional Jet A-1 blended with pure SAF.
In this first phase, Thailand’s rules limit SAF production to HEFA (Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids) technology.
For comparison, the European Union has enforced mandatory SAF blending for flights departing from EU airports, with a 2% blending requirement in place since 2025.
text:
Thailand’s sustainable aviation fuel industry is shifting from early projects to a rule-based market. The Department of Energy Business is preparing to introduce new SAF standards and to make blending mandatory in jet fuel from 2026. The regulations are set to come into force on January 1, 2026. Under the framework, Jet A-1 fuel specifications and quality requirements at both production and sale stages will be split into three categories: conventional Jet A-1 fuel, fuel produced through co-hydroprocessing, and conventional Jet A-1 blended with pure SAF. The department has also defined standards for SAF itself, aiming to ensure SAF produced and supplied in Thailand meets recognised international standards.

In this first phase, Thailand’s rules limit SAF production to HEFA (Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids) technology. Feedstocks and production processes must comply with ASTM D7566 norms. Officials have framed this as a practical step, since Alcohol-to-Jet technology using ethanol is still under development and has not yet reached full commercial scale. The policy also aligns with ICAO efforts to encourage airlines worldwide to adopt SAF to reduce aviation emissions. Globally, aviation is responsible for approximately 2% of total carbon dioxide emissions and accounts for 12% of emissions from the transportation sector, underscoring why standards, traceability, and fuel quality are central to adoption.

Projects, Blending Timelines, and the Commercial Supply Base

Thailand already has projects that can anchor early supply as blending begins. Bangchak Corporation is building a HEFA SAF plant using used cooking oil as the primary feedstock. The project is designed for one million litres per day, or about 6,289 barrels per day, and is expected to be completed and begin commercial operations in the second quarter of 2026. PTT Global Chemical (GC) is producing SAF using co-processing HEFA technology, also based on used cooking oil, and the project is already operating commercially with an initial capacity of 16,438 litres per day, or about 103 barrels per day. These volumes matter because mandated blending creates predictable demand that can support ramp-up.

Thailand’s first SAF standard has been reported as expected to be released and enforced with blending that starts at 1% and increases to 8% by 2036. The move is positioned to decarbonize aviation in line with international measures and to support Thailand’s goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. For comparison, the European Union has enforced mandatory SAF blending for flights departing from EU airports, with a 2% blending requirement in place since 2025. These policy signals matter in a market that is still scaling globally, where SAF can be blended with conventional fuels at levels ranging from 10% to 50% depending on production method and feedstock.

Broader market indicators highlight why Thailand’s direction is attracting attention, even as local production ramps up in stages. Fortune Business Insights valued the global SAF market at USD 2.72 billion in 2025 and projected growth from USD 4.02 billion in 2026 to USD 40.09 billion by 2034, with a CAGR of 33.3%. In Asia-Pacific, BIS Research estimated the SAF market could reach $39.23 billion by 2033 from $0.38 billion in 2023, at a growth rate of 58.99% over 2023–2033. Regional supply potential is also being discussed: an ASEAN outlook cited SAF feedstocks such as used cooking oil, rice waste, cassava waste, and forestry residues, and noted HEFA is the most prevalent technology for producing SAF today, costing about twice as much as jet fuel, with feedstock the largest cost contributor.
